desc: OpenBao before 2.6.3 contains an information disclosure vulnerability that allows attackers to leak sensitive data into audit logs by sending malformed plugin parameters. Attackers can submit requests with malformed TypeKVPair or TypeHeader field values, causing error messages containing sensitive input to be recorded in audit logs.

title: OpenBao before 2.6.4 and 2.7.x before 2.7.1 fails to write response audit entries for the unauthenticated sys/generate-root, sys/rekey, and sys/rekey-recovery-key endpoints when…
desc: OpenBao before 2.6.4 and 2.7.x before 2.7.1 fails to write response audit entries for the unauthenticated sys/generate-root, sys/rekey, and sys/rekey-recovery-key endpoints when request audit logging succeeds but response audit logging fails. An attacker using these endpoints can complete root token generation or rekey operations without a corresponding response audit record, hindering forensic detection.

An authenticated attacker can keep renewing such tokens to persist access after the Kubernetes service account has been deleted.

desc: Mistune before 3.3.0 contains a path traversal vulnerability in the RST include directive that allows attackers to read arbitrary files by supplying relative or absolute paths. Attackers can submit markdown containing include directives referencing ../ sequences or absolute paths to embed sensitive files like credentials or environment data in rendered HTML.

Attackers can send small markdown payloads that trigger O(N^2) parse_link_text and parse_link_label probing, occupying rendering workers for 30+ seconds per 16 KB input.

Attackers can append declarations like background:url() to the rendered figure style attribute, forcing victim browsers to send requests to attacker servers and leak attribute values.

desc: Mistune before 3.3.0 contains a cross-site scripting vulnerability in the Include directive that emits included .html, .xhtml, or .htm file content as raw block_html tokens. Attackers who can plant an HTML file readable by the renderer can reference it via an include directive, combined with path traversal, to execute stored scripts when escape=False is set.

desc: Mistune from 3.0.0 before 3.3.0 contains an algorithmic complexity denial of service vulnerability in the parse_link_text function in src/mistune/helpers.py. Attackers can submit markdown with deeply nested square brackets triggering quadratic parsing time, exhausting server CPU with small crafted requests.

title: libmongocrypt builds requests to external key management services (AWS, Azure and GCP) by inserting values from key vault documents, KMS provider configuration and KMS responses…
desc: libmongocrypt builds requests to external key management services (AWS, Azure and GCP) by inserting values from key vault documents, KMS provider configuration and KMS responses into request lines, headers and signed request bodies without validating or encoding them for each context. A user with write access to the key vault collection can alter the structure of these requests, including adding members to request bodies and token claims that the library then signs with the application's credentials. This may result in key management operations being performed with parameters the application did not intend.

title: A numeric-type conversion flaw in the BSON handling library of the MongoDB C# Driver allows an out-of-range binary subtype value supplied through untrusted textual input to…
desc: A numeric-type conversion flaw in the BSON handling library of the MongoDB C# Driver allows an out-of-range binary subtype value supplied through untrusted textual input to bypass the library's binary-element integrity checks. When such a value is later encoded, it is narrowed to a smaller wire representation, producing binary elements that misdeclare their type or length. An unauthenticated party able to supply text parsed by an affected application can cause it to emit and persist malformed binary data, which subsequent readers either reject with an error or silently interpret as shorter than the data that was validated.

title: A client-side encryption schema construction component in the MongoDB C# Driver places caller-supplied field identifiers into a position that is interpreted as a pattern…
desc: A client-side encryption schema construction component in the MongoDB C# Driver places caller-supplied field identifiers into a position that is interpreted as a pattern expression, without normalizing or validating them. As a result, an application that designates certain fields for client-side field-level encryption may have the protection silently fail to apply, so data intended to be encrypted is stored and returned in cleartext; conversely, the rule may apply more broadly than intended. No user action is required to cause the condition, and any party with ordinary read access to the stored data — without possession of the encryption keys — can observe the unprotected values.

title: A data-query-logic neutralization weakness in the update-statement construction component of the MongoDB C# Driver can cause application-supplied values to be interpreted as…
desc: A data-query-logic neutralization weakness in the update-statement construction component of the MongoDB C# Driver can cause application-supplied values to be interpreted as query/update logic rather than as literal data. An application user who can influence the content of values that the application passes into the affected builder surface, without any special privilege beyond ordinary read-write application access, may cause stored data to be modified or removed in ways the application never intended. The result is unauthorized integrity impact on the affected application data; there is no direct loss of confidentiality or availability of the database service.

title: A memory-handling weakness in the BSON deserialization component of the MongoDB C# Driver may cause data left over from previously processed content to be returned when specially…
desc: A memory-handling weakness in the BSON deserialization component of the MongoDB C# Driver may cause data left over from previously processed content to be returned when specially crafted serialized input is parsed. An unauthenticated party able to supply serialized data to an application that maps certain primitive collection types can cause residual bytes from unrelated data processed earlier on the same execution thread to be surfaced as legitimate values. This can result in disclosure of a limited amount of information belonging to other requests or principals of the consuming application. No authentication or special privileges within the application are required.

title: A flaw in the client-side encryption support of the MongoDB .NET/C# driver can cause data designated for client-side field-level encryption to be written without encryption.
desc: A flaw in the client-side encryption support of the MongoDB .NET/C# driver can cause data designated for client-side field-level encryption to be written without encryption. Under certain platform text-encoding configurations, an internal name conversion loses information, so the encryption layer fails to associate the operation with its configured encryption rules and the operation proceeds without an error being raised. An application user with the ability to write data through an affected application can therefore have sensitive fields persisted in plaintext, defeating the confidentiality guarantee that client-side encryption is intended to provide. No integrity or availability impact was observed.

title: The MongoDB C# Driver compares TLS client certificates by issuer and serial number only when deciding whether two clients can share cached connections.
desc: The MongoDB C# Driver compares TLS client certificates by issuer and serial number only when deciding whether two clients can share cached connections. In an application that creates clients from certificates supplied by different users, a user who provides a certificate copying another user's issuer and serial number, without that user's private key, can be given connections authenticated with the other user's certificate. Database operations can then run under the other user's identity, affecting the confidentiality and integrity of data that identity can access.

title: The MongoDB C# Driver does not neutralize dot and dollar characters in dictionary keys, field names and array-filter identifiers used in LINQ queries before placing them into the…
desc: The MongoDB C# Driver does not neutralize dot and dollar characters in dictionary keys, field names and array-filter identifiers used in LINQ queries before placing them into the field paths it sends to the server. An application user whose input reaches these positions can redirect a query or update to fields the application did not name, which can expose other users' documents and widen updates beyond the intended data. Certain values can also write malformed fields that leave stored documents unreadable by the application until they are repaired.

title: The MongoDB C# Driver does not reject replacement documents whose top-level field names begin with a dollar sign in FindOneAndReplace, unlike other replace operations.
desc: The MongoDB C# Driver does not reject replacement documents whose top-level field names begin with a dollar sign in FindOneAndReplace, unlike other replace operations. An application that builds such a document from user-supplied field names can have the server apply update operators instead of a full replacement. The effect is limited to the document matched by the application's own filter, whose contents can be modified in ways the application did not intend.

title: A data-validation flaw exists in the BSON handling and binary serialization path of the MongoDB C# Driver.
desc: A data-validation flaw exists in the BSON handling and binary serialization path of the MongoDB C# Driver. When an application constructs a raw or lazy BSON document object from externally supplied binary data, the driver does not verify that the size quantity declared inside that data matches the amount of data actually provided, and it copies the data onto the wire unchanged. An unauthenticated party who can supply binary content to such an application can thereby cause additional elements to be inserted into, or existing elements to be removed from, the database command the application issues, without needing any database credentials of their own. This can result in unauthorized modification of stored data and disclosure of data outside the intended scope of the application's request, bounded by the database privileges the application itself holds.

title: A 32-bit integer wraparound in the MongoDB C Driver's Windows-only Kerberos/SSPI authentication code can cause an undersized heap buffer to be allocated when an excessively long…
desc: A 32-bit integer wraparound in the MongoDB C Driver's Windows-only Kerberos/SSPI authentication code can cause an undersized heap buffer to be allocated when an excessively long credential value is supplied in the client's connection configuration. A party able to control that client-side configuration, in conjunction with the affected authentication mechanism, can cause the driver to write outside the bounds of the allocated buffer. This may result in corruption of client process memory and denial of service of the client application. The issue affects only client builds compiled with the Windows-native authentication backend.

title: The MongoDB C# Driver's BSON library contains an uncontrolled resource consumption weakness in its deserialization handling of one BSON value type.
desc: The MongoDB C# Driver's BSON library contains an uncontrolled resource consumption weakness in its deserialization handling of one BSON value type. An application that deserializes untrusted content with the library retains data derived from that content for the lifetime of the process, with no limit on how much accumulates. An unauthenticated remote party who can cause such content to be deserialized can drive unbounded memory growth, exhausting the host application's available memory and denying service. There is no impact to confidentiality or integrity, and no MongoDB server component is affected.

title: The MongoDB C# Driver writes GeoJSON extra members without checking whether their names collide with reserved GeoJSON members such as type and coordinates.
desc: The MongoDB C# Driver writes GeoJSON extra members without checking whether their names collide with reserved GeoJSON members such as type and coordinates. An application that places user-supplied field names into these extra members can store documents with duplicate geometry fields, so the server and the driver resolve different values for the same record. Affected records can also become unreadable through the driver, interrupting application code that reads them.

title: OCO-Server is a self-hosted endpoint management application for computer inventory, software deployment, and mobile device management.
desc: OCO-Server is a self-hosted endpoint management application for computer inventory, software deployment, and mobile device management. Prior to 1.2.3,the Apple MDM enrollment endpoint `frontend/api-mdm.php` verifies the signed enrollment-request plist with `openssl_pkcs7_verify(..., PKCS7_NOVERIFY, ...)`. `PKCS7_NOVERIFY` disables signer certificate chain and trust validation, so the signature only has to be self-consistent with whatever certificate is embedded in the PKCS#7 blob. A self-signed certificate from an unrelated attacker is accepted. Because the endpoint trusts the `SERIAL` field taken from the unverified payload, anyone who knows a registered device's serial number can sign a forged plist (`SERIAL` = victim device, attacker-chosen `UDID`) with an arbitrary self-signed certificate; POST it unauthenticated to `/api-mdm.php/profile` (Content-Type: `application/pkcs7-signature`); and receive the victim device's freshly minted MDM identity: a certificate with `CN=<serial>` issued by the server's internal MDM device CA, bundled with its private key in a PKCS#12 payload inside the returned `.mobileconfig` enrollment profile. Additionally, the victim's `mobile_device` database row is silently overwritten with the attacker-supplied `UDID` (device-record hijack). With the stolen certificate and key, the attacker can impersonate the victim device on all subsequent MDM traffic (`/checkin`, `/mdm`, `/parameters`), which authenticate callers by the certificate CN (the serial number) via `checkSignature()` in the same file. This yields control over the victim device's MDM relationship: reading its management data, replacing its push token, and disrupting or redirecting its enrollment. Version 1.2.3 fixes the issue.

title: draw.io Desktop is the official Electron build of draw.io.
desc: draw.io Desktop is the official Electron build of draw.io. Prior to 31.4.4, draw.io Desktop is vulnerable to arbitrary local-file disclosure through the Electron main process's read-side IPC handlers. The readFile, getFileDrafts, getBkpFile, fileStat, isFileWritable, checkFileExists, and watchFile actions operate on a renderer-chosen filesystem path with no blessed-path (assertWritablePath) authorization. The only gates are validateSender — a URL-prefix origin check — plus, for readFile alone, a content "sniff" and a lexical appBaseDir prefix block. The write-side handlers (saveFile, writeFile, saveDraft, deleteFile) are all protected by assertWritablePath; the read side is not. The result is a read/write authorization asymmetry: any frame executing in the app's file:// origin can read the contents of local files that the same origin is explicitly forbidden to write. This issue is fixed in version 31.4.4.

title: OpenTelemetry Python provides the Python API and SDK for OpenTelemetry.
desc: OpenTelemetry Python provides the Python API and SDK for OpenTelemetry. Prior to 1.45.1, the opentelemetry-api function TraceState.from_header in opentelemetry/trace/span.py, reached through TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract, parses inbound W3C tracestate headers with an unbounded optional-whitespace regular expression. A malformed header containing a long run of spaces or tabs without a following comma causes quadratic backtracking before the member-count limit is applied. Services using the default W3C Trace Context propagator can therefore spend excessive CPU time on one unauthenticated request when the HTTP server, parser, gateway, or custom carrier accepts a sufficiently large header. The processing can occupy a synchronous worker or delay unrelated requests on the same asynchronous event loop. The impact is limited to availability and does not expose or modify telemetry data or allow code execution. This issue is fixed in version 1.45.1.

title: tarfile.tar_filter could be bypassed using crafted link entries, including symlinks with empty or directory-like names, to redirect later archive members outside the intended…
desc:
tarfile.tar_filter could be bypassed using crafted link entries, including symlinks with empty or directory-like names, to redirect later archive members outside the intended extraction directory. This allowed a malicious tar archive to cause tarfile.extractall() with filter="tar" to write files outside the destination directory, subject to the permissions of the extracting process.

This is the tarfile.tar_filter counterpart of CVE-2026-7774, which covered tarfile.data_filter.

title: Missing Authorization (CWE-862) in the user API of Roskus Prospero Flow CRM from 2.0.0 before 5.26.0 allows a user with a basic role to read the accounts of other users of its…
desc: Missing Authorization (CWE-862) in the user API of Roskus Prospero Flow CRM from 2.0.0 before 5.26.0 allows a user with a basic role to read the accounts of other users of its own company, including accounts with higher privileges, and, in versions from 3.5.0, to delete them, because the routes GET /api/user/{id} and DELETE /api/user/{id} in routes/api.php carry only the auth:api middleware, which checks that a JSON Web Token is valid and nothing more, and neither UserReadController::read() nor UserDeleteController::delete() checks a permission, a policy or a role before acting. Object access is scoped by company: the read path limits the query to the company of the authenticated user, and the delete path compares the company of the target account with the company of the authenticated user. The delete path skips that comparison when the company of the authenticated user is Company::DEFAULT_COMPANY, so a user with a basic role in that company can delete any account of any company of the installation. Deleting an account removes the data held on it, and the last administrative account of a company can be deleted. This gives the attacker the personal data held on the other accounts, including email address, telephone number, postal address and IBAN, and the ability to delete accounts it has no permission to administer.

title: OCO-Server is a self-hosted endpoint management application for computer inventory, software deployment, and mobile device management.
desc: OCO-Server is a self-hosted endpoint management application for computer inventory, software deployment, and mobile device management. Prior to 1.2.3, a valid Self-Service Portal user with permission to create job containers and read visibility on a computer and package can queue an uninstall job without deploy permission for those resources. Requests to `self-service/ajax-handler/job-containers.php` pass `uninstall_package_assignment_id[]` values to `lib/SelfService/CoreLogic.class.php::uninstallSelfService()`. Its permission-check loop continues after denied `METHOD_DEPLOY` checks without removing rejected IDs from `$installationIds`, then passes the original list to `lib/CoreLogic.class.php::uninstall()`. The CoreLogic object is constructed with a null SystemUser, causing `lib/CoreLogic.class.php::checkPermission()` to treat the operation as system context and unconditionally permit it. Enumerable `computer_package.id` values allow selection of readable installed-package assignments, including those on other users' computers. The `deploySelfService()` install path instead aborts on denied deployment permission, and resources lacking read permission remain blocked. This permits unauthorized software-removal jobs across resources visible to the acting user's role. This issue is fixed in version 1.2.3.

desc: Missing authorization in the PAM AD computer import endpoint in Devolutions Server 2026.3.5.0 through 2026.3.10.0 and 2026.2.20.0 and earlier allows an authenticated non-administrative user with a PAM license to create PAM sub-providers under existing AD providers via a crafted import request.

desc: Incorrect authorization in the Devolutions Gateway token generation in Devolutions Server 2026.3.10.0  and earlier allows an authenticated non-administrative attacker to bypass the Network Access Rules of a virtual gateway and reach denied hosts via wildcard additional destinations signed into the gateway token.

title: GitPython validates a submodule's ".git" path only after cloning into it (RCE)
desc:
### Summary


`create_submodule(name, path, url)` clones a submodule into the repo's own `.git`
directory before it rejects the path. A `path` of ".git/hooks" is accepted by the
pre-clone check, so the submodule is cloned straight into the live hooks directory,
and a file named `post-checkout` in the submodule becomes an executable
`.git/hooks/post-checkout`. On 3.2.0+ the later index check does raise `ValueError`,
but only after the clone already wrote to disk, and it does not remove the planted
hook; on 3.1.x there is no such check and the call succeeds silently. Either way the
hook runs on the next git operation (e.g. checkout), giving code execution.

### Details


The checkout path is validated too late, after the clone has already mutated disk.
This breaks the "validate before mutation" invariant that commit 43a43cd8 ("Validate
submodule checkout and metadata paths before mutation") set out to enforce.

Submodule.add() calls the permissive path check before cloning, and the strict check
only reaches the ".git" alias at index time, after _clone_repo has written to disk:

git/objects/submodule/base.py (Submodule.add)
  599: path = cls._to_relative_path(repo, path)           # accepts ".git/hooks"
  673: mrepo = cls._clone_repo(repo, url, path, name, ...) # clones into <worktree>/.git/hooks
  714: index.add([sm], write=True)                         # strict check only triggers here

git/index/base.py (IndexFile._preprocess_add_items)
  732: _validate_repo_path(entry.path)                     # rejects ".git", too late

_to_relative_path only blocks `..`/absolute/out-of-tree paths; `.git` aliases are
rejected only by _validate_repo_path, which was added in 3.2.0 (commit a75aedf3) and
runs at the index boundary. The ValueError it raises at line 732 does not roll back
what _clone_repo already wrote.

Version-dependent behavior:
- 3.2.0 .. tip bda18e08: _validate_repo_path raises ValueError at index.add, but the
  hook is already on disk and is not removed (incorrect order of validation vs. clone).
- 3.1.x (e.g. 3.1.59): _validate_repo_path does not exist and _to_relative_path does
  not reject `.git`; create_submodule(path=".git/hooks", ...) returns with no error at
  all and the hook is planted silently.

### Proof of concept


Setup:
  evilsub/ : a git repo whose ROOT contains an executable file named post-checkout (the payload)
  victim/  : a git repo with at least 1 commit and a second branch, whose .git/hooks has NO
             sample hooks (the state of a minimal/CI checkout, or `git init` with an empty
             template dir, or GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR/init.templateDir empty)

import git, os.path as osp
try:
    git.Repo("victim").create_submodule(name="x", path=".git/hooks", url=osp.abspath("evilsub"))
except ValueError:
    pass   # 3.2.0+: ".git" is rejected, but only AFTER the clone, so the plant already happened.
           # 3.1.x: no exception is raised at all; the call succeeds and still plants the hook.

#### victim/.git/hooks/post-checkout now exists, mode 0755, attacker-controlled, on every
#### affected version. Any later checkout runs it:
####  git -C victim checkout <other-branch>   ->   the hook runs   ->   code execution

Verified live:
- tip bda18e08 (3.2.0 + 3 commits): create_submodule raised ValueError from
  git/index/base.py:732, yet .git/hooks/post-checkout was present and executable, and
  `git checkout` executed it.
- 3.1.59: create_submodule returned with no error; .git/hooks/post-checkout was planted
  and executed by `git checkout`.

### Impact

Arbitrary code execution. A library/app that creates a submodule from an
attacker-influenced `path` ends up with an attacker-controlled executable in
`.git/hooks`, which git runs on ordinary later operations. This affects any service
that derives a submodule checkout path from untrusted data, e.g. one that ingests a
submodule spec (name/path/url) from a user-supplied manifest or API request and feeds
`path` into create_submodule. On 3.2.0+ the library's own validation is the thing that
fails: it correctly rejects the `.git` path, but only after the submodule has already
been cloned into place, so an app that traps the ValueError reasonably believes the
unsafe path was blocked.

Preconditions (hence AC:H): (1) the app passes an attacker-influenced submodule `path`;
(2) the target hook name is free in `.git/hooks`, true for minimal/CI/container
checkouts and whenever init.templateDir/GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR is empty. With the default
sample hooks present, `git clone` refuses the non-empty destination and no plant occurs.

Affected: all tested versions from 3.1.x (3.1.59) through the current tip bda18e08
(3.2.0 + 3 commits). 3.1.x plants silently; 3.2.0+ plants despite raising ValueError.

title: toml-node: Uncontrolled resource consumption (CPU DoS) via unbounded-length integer literals in toml.parse()
desc:
### Summary
`toml.parse()` converts integer literals (hex, octal, binary, and decimal) to `BigInt` without first bounding the length of the digit sequence. Since `BigInt(string)` construction from a very long numeric string runs in super-linear time, a single small, well-formed TOML document containing one long integer literal can pin a Node.js process's event loop at 100% CPU for several seconds — a denial of service for any application that parses attacker-supplied or third-party TOML. No authentication or complex crafting is required.

### Details
In `lib/parser.js`, the grammar actions that build integer nodes call `BigInt()` directly on the matched digit text, with no upper bound on its length:

- `lib/parser.js:326` — hex: `BigInt('0x' + stripUnderscores(digits))`
- `lib/parser.js:327` — octal: `BigInt('0o' + stripUnderscores(digits))`
- `lib/parser.js:328` — binary: `BigInt('0b' + stripUnderscores(digits))`
- `lib/parser.js:329` — decimal: `BigInt(stripUnderscores(text))`

The parser does enforce a nesting-depth limit (`MAX_DEPTH`, default 500, `lib/parser.js:4343`) to guard against stack overflow from deeply nested arrays/inline tables (per GHSA-82x6-q7mm-w9cf). However, that guard only bounds *structural nesting* — it does not bound the length of a single scalar token.

The subsequent 64-bit range check in `lib/compiler.js` (`reduceInteger`, lines 143–150, comparing against `INT64_MIN` / `INT64_MAX` defined at lines 3–4) happens **after** the expensive `BigInt()` conversion has already completed. It therefore provides no protection against this cost — the CPU time is already spent by the time the value is rejected as out of range.

### PoC

```js
const toml = require('toml');

const N = 5_000_000; // ~5 MB request body
const doc = 'x = 0x' + 'f'.repeat(N);

const start = Date.now();
try {
  toml.parse(doc); // eventually throws "outside the 64-bit signed integer range" —
                    // but only after the costly conversion has run
} catch (e) {}

console.log('elapsed:', Date.now() - start, 'ms');
```

**Measured results:**

| Digits (hex) | Approx. payload size | Parse time |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 200,000 | ~200 KB | 141 ms |
| 400,000 | ~400 KB | 276 ms |
| 800,000 | ~800 KB | 685 ms |
| 1,600,000 | ~1.6 MB | 1,761 ms |
| 5,000,000 | ~5 MB | 6,061 ms |

Growth is clearly super-linear. The same behavior reproduces for plain decimal literals (3,000,000 `'9'` digits → ~6.3 s).

### Impact
Any application that calls `toml.parse()` on untrusted or third-party input — config upload endpoints, CI/CD tools ingesting user-supplied `.toml` files, package managers, linters, editors/language servers — is exposed.

During the conversion, the event loop is fully blocked. In a typical single-threaded Node.js server this stalls **all** concurrent request handling, not just the request containing the malicious payload. A single ~5 MB request is sufficient to cause several seconds of full CPU denial of service.

**Suggested fix:** Reject digit sequences above a reasonable length *before* calling `BigInt()`, analogous to the existing `maxDepth` option. A 64-bit signed integer requires at most 20 decimal digits or 16 hex digits, so any digit sequence significantly longer than that is guaranteed to fail the existing range check anyway, and can be rejected with a cheap `.length` comparison instead of paying for the full `BigInt` conversion.

title: toml-node: Quadratic-complexity DoS via long dotted keys or table paths in toml.parse()
desc:
## Summary

`toml.parse()` is vulnerable to a quadratic-complexity (O(n²)) denial-of-service via a single
long dotted key, table header, or inline-table key. A ~100KB crafted document causes a
multi-second synchronous hang; a ~200KB document crashes the Node.js process outright with an
uncatchable out-of-memory error. This is a separate, unpatched code path from the previously
fixed stack-overflow DoS (`GHSA-82x6-q7mm-w9cf`) — it requires no array/inline-table nesting at
all, and is confirmed unaffected by the `maxDepth` option that fixed that earlier issue.

## Affected component / version

- Package: `toml` (npm), repository `BinaryMuse/toml-node`
- Functions: `assign()`, `deepRef()`, `setNestedKey()` in `lib/compiler.js`
- Confirmed present in the audited checkout at commit `1b2ac40` (2026-07-16), one commit past
  the `v5.0.0` tag (a changelog-only change) — i.e. present in `v5.0.0`, the latest release.
  Not exhaustively verified against every prior release, but the affected functions are
  unrelated to `v5.0.0`'s BigInt/Temporal changes (per `CHANGELOG.md`), so the defect likely
  predates that release as well.

## Details

`toml.parse(input, options)` (`index.js:5-9`) forwards the caller-supplied string to
`parser.parse()` and then `compiler.compile()` with no length or structural validation.
Inside `lib/compiler.js`, three separate functions each walk a dotted key's segments in a
`for` loop and, on **every** iteration, recompute the full path-prefix string from scratch:

- `assign()` (lines 69-107, the sink at line 81): `var intermediatePath =
  makeFullPath(keys.slice(0, i + 1));` — reached for top-level dotted-key assignments like
  `a.b.c = 1`.
- `deepRef()` (lines 247-281, the sink at line 252): the identical pattern via
  `pathKey(keys.slice(0, i + 1))` — reached from table headers `[a.b.c]` and array-of-tables
  `[[a.b.c]]` via `setPath()`/`addTableArray()`.
- `setNestedKey()` (lines 184-202, the sink at line 187): the identical pattern — reached from
  inline-table dotted keys like `t = { a.b.c = 1 }`.

`keys.slice(0, i + 1)` allocates a new array of length `i`; `pathKey()`/`makeFullPath()`
(lines 311-317) then does `.map(quoteDottedString).join(".")`, also O(i). Since this runs on
every one of the `n` segments of a dotted key, total work is `O(1 + 2 + ... + n) = O(n²)`, not
`O(n)`. The string is computed unconditionally on the happy path (only ever *used* if an error
is about to be thrown), so there is no early exit that makes this cheap in practice.

No limit exists anywhere on dotted-key segment count: `dot_ended_table_key_part+` and
`inline_dot_key_part+` in `src/toml.pegjs` (lines 122, 311) are unbounded `+` repetitions,
parsed iteratively rather than through the grammar's `value` rule — so the existing
`MAX_DEPTH`/`maxDepth` nesting guard (`src/toml.pegjs:141-151`, enforced in the generated
`lib/parser.js:1022`) does not apply to key length at all. We confirmed this directly: setting
`options.maxDepth: 1` (the strictest possible value) against a 16,000-segment key produced no
measurable timing difference from the unrestricted case.

## Proof of Concept

```js
const toml = require('toml');

// n-segment dotted key: "k0.k1.k2. ... .k{n-1} = 1"
function segKey(n) {
  const parts = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) parts.push('k' + i);
  return parts.join('.') + ' = 1\n';
}

// ~100.9 KB input -- takes ~6.6-6.8 seconds
toml.parse(segKey(16000));

// ~200 KB input -- crashes the Node process:
// "FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit - JavaScript heap out of memory"
toml.parse(segKey(32000));
```

Measured timings (Node v22, direct execution against this repo):

| n (segments) | input size | time |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | ~4.9 KB | 34 ms |
| 8,000 | ~46.9 KB | 1.6 s |
| 16,000 | ~100.9 KB | 6.8 s |
| 32,000 | ~200 KB | **process crash (OOM)** |

Doubling `n` from 8,000→16,000 roughly quadruples runtime (~4.2x), the signature of O(n²)
rather than the expected O(n) (~2x). Independently reproduced with the identical scaling
signature for the table-header variant (`[k0. ... .k15999]`, exercising `deepRef()`) and the
inline-table variant (`t = { k0. ... .k15999 = 1 }`, exercising `setNestedKey()`).

We also generalized this into a property-based fuzzing harness (fast-check, run under Node)
that automatically tests the "doubling input size should not more than roughly double parse
time" invariant across 12 structural dimensions of the grammar/compiler; it independently
re-flags all three code paths above on every run, with no additional dimension confirmed
vulnerable after follow-up investigation. The harness is available on request.

## Impact

Node.js is single-threaded — a synchronous multi-second-to-crashing `parse()` call blocks the
entire event loop of the process calling it, stalling every other request/operation that
process is handling, not just the attacker's own. At the upper end this is not merely a hang:
an uncaught, process-terminating out-of-memory crash from a ~200KB attacker-supplied string is
a full denial of service requiring no authentication — just the ability to get one string
parsed by an application using this library (config upload, API request body, imported
manifest, or any of this library's intended use cases).

## Suggested remediation

Build the path prefix as an incrementally-extended string as the loop walks each segment
(append one already-quoted segment per iteration to a running string) instead of re-slicing an
array and re-joining the entire prefix from scratch on every iteration. For example, in
`assign()`:

```js
function assign(node) {
  var keys = node.key;
  var value = node.value;
  var off = node.offset;
  if (!Array.isArray(keys)) keys = [keys];
  var reduced = reduceValueNode(value);

  var target = context;
  var pathStr = pathKey(currentPath); // computed once, not per segment
  for (var i = 0; i < keys.length - 1; i++) {
    var k = keys[i];
    var quotedK = quoteDottedString(k);
    var intermediatePath = pathStr ? pathStr + "." + quotedK : quotedK; // O(new segment), not O(i)
    pathStr = intermediatePath;
    // ...same conditional logic as today, using intermediatePath
    target = target[k];
  }
  // ...
}
```

The identical treatment applies to `deepRef()` and `setNestedKey()`. As defense-in-depth,
consider also capping total key-segment count or overall input size, the same way `maxDepth`
already caps nesting.


## Credit

Discovered and reported by SecDim Security Research
secdim.com | @secdim | security@secdim.com

title: toml-node: Prototype pollution: parsing a TOML document can write to Object.prototype
desc:
### Summary
CVE-2026-63376 described prototype pollution through __proto__ key-path desynchronization and was fixed in 4.1.2 by rewriting the path bookkeeping and adding an ownedContainers WeakSet. The desynchronization is still reachable, spelled with a quote character instead of a dot, and the owned-container check is not applied on the path that matters.

A four-line TOML document parsed with toml.parse() writes a property onto Object.prototype, where it is visible to every object in the process — including objects produced by unrelated libraries.

### Details
Three gaps compose. All line numbers are `lib/compiler.js` in 5.0.0.

**1. The path-key encoding is ambiguous.** `quoteDottedString()` quotes a segment only when it contains a `.`, and never escapes a `"` inside the segment:

```js
287:  function quoteDottedString(str) {
288:    if (str.indexOf(".") > -1) {
289:      return "\"" + str + "\"";
290:    } else {
291:      return str;
292:    }
293:  }
```

So the key path `['x.y']` and the key path `['"x', 'y"']` both render as the string `"x.y"`. This is the same desynchronization CVE-2026-63376 named, with a quote in place of the dot.

**2. A table-array header can clear another key's guard.** `addTableArray()` walks `assignedPaths` / `valueAssignments` with `isSameOrSubPath()` over those ambiguous strings, so a header whose rendered path collides with an unrelated key deletes that key's entry.

**3. The descent in `assign()` has no owned-container check.** `deepRef()` applies `isOwnedContainer()` only to intermediate segments (`lib/compiler.js:265`, `:273`) and returns the final container unchecked. `assign()` then walks it with only a shape test:

```js
 93:      target = target[k];
...
103:    target[lastKey] = reduced;
```

A TOML datetime is a `Date`. It satisfies `typeof target[k] === "object"` and is not an array, so the walk descends into it — and a `Date` has a live prototype chain to `Object.prototype`.

Putting the three together, a document can make the current table a `Date` and then walk `__proto__.__proto__` to `Object.prototype`.

```bash
mkdir poc && cd poc && npm init -y >/dev/null && npm install toml@5.0.0
```

```toml
# poc.toml
"b.c" = 1979-05-27T07:32:00Z
[['"b']]
["b.c"]
__proto__.__proto__.polluted = "yes"
```

Line 1 defines a key whose rendered path is `"b.c"` and whose value is a `Date`.
Line 2 is a table-array header whose rendered path collides with it, clearing its guard.
Line 3 re-enters that key, so the current table is now the `Date`.
Line 4 walks `Date` → `Date.prototype` → `Object.prototype`.

```js
// poc.js
const toml = require('toml');
const fs = require('fs');

console.log('before:', JSON.stringify(({}).polluted));
toml.parse(fs.readFileSync('poc.toml', 'utf8'));
console.log('after: ', JSON.stringify(({}).polluted));
console.log('Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty("polluted") =', Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty('polluted'));
console.log('JSON.parse("{}").polluted =', JSON.stringify(JSON.parse('{}').polluted));
```

```
$ node poc.js
before: undefined
after:  "yes"
Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty("polluted") = true
JSON.parse("{}").polluted = "yes"
```

The payload sets a single harmless marker property. The last line shows the property is visible on an object this code never touched.

A useful control: the same document without line 2 (the guard-clearing header) is correctly rejected on 4.1.2 and later, which confirms the clearing step is what is load-bearing.

### Impact

Any application that parses a TOML document from an untrusted source is affected — a configuration file uploaded by a user, a manifest from a third-party package or repository, a document posted to an API. Prototype pollution of this kind commonly escalates to authentication or authorization bypass, denial of service, and in applications with a suitable gadget, remote code execution, because every object in the process inherits the injected property.

Suggested fix: in `assign()`, apply the same check the intermediate descent already uses — after `target = target[k]`, reject when `!isOwnedContainer(target)`. Equivalently, apply `isOwnedContainer` to the value `deepRef()` returns. Separately, `quoteDottedString()` should escape `"` inside a segment so that distinct key paths cannot render to the same string.

title: toml-node: Quadratic-complexity DoS via many array-of-tables headers in toml.parse()
desc:
## Summary

`toml.parse()` is vulnerable to a quadratic-complexity (O(n²)) denial-of-service via many
array-of-tables (`[[name]]`) headers. `addTableArray()` in `lib/compiler.js` rescans two
entire bookkeeping Sets on every `[[name]]` header without pruning unrelated or distinct
entries, so a document containing n such headers costs O(n²) compiler work. A ~321KB document
of 20,000 distinct-named `[[name]]` blocks takes ~10.3 seconds to parse — a completely
ordinary-looking TOML shape (a flat settings block plus one or more array-of-tables sections),
not a contrived edge case. This is a separate, unpatched code path from the previously fixed
stack-overflow DoS (`GHSA-82x6-q7mm-w9cf`) and requires no key nesting or dotted keys at all.

## Affected component / version

- Package: `toml` (npm), repository `BinaryMuse/toml-node`
- Function: `addTableArray()` in `lib/compiler.js`
- Confirmed present in the audited checkout at commit `1b2ac40` (2026-07-16), one commit past
  the `v5.0.0` tag (a changelog-only change) — i.e. present in `v5.0.0`, the latest release.
  Not exhaustively verified against every prior release, but the affected function is
  unrelated to `v5.0.0`'s BigInt/Temporal changes (per `CHANGELOG.md`), so the defect likely
  predates that release as well.

## Details

`toml.parse(input, options)` (`index.js:5-9`) forwards the caller-supplied string to
`parser.parse()` and then `compiler.compile()` with no length or structural validation. Every
`[[name]]` (array-of-tables) header is routed (`reduce()`, `lib/compiler.js:43`) to
`addTableArray()` (`lib/compiler.js:218-245`), which performs two full linear scans on every
call:

```js
assignedPaths.forEach(function(p) {
  if (isSameOrSubPath(p, quotedPath)) assignedPaths.delete(p);
});
valueAssignments.forEach(function(p) {
  if (isSameOrSubPath(p, quotedPath)) valueAssignments.delete(p);
});
```
(`lib/compiler.js:228-233`)

`assignedPaths` and `valueAssignments` accumulate one entry per top-level key/table/array path
ever assigned in the entire document. Each scan prunes only entries matching the *currently
reopened* path via `isSameOrSubPath()` (`lib/compiler.js:319-321`: `path === prefix ||
path.indexOf(prefix + ".") === 0`); anything else — an unrelated top-level key, or simply a
*different* array-of-tables name — is never removed and is rescanned in full on every
subsequent `[[name]]` header for the rest of the parse. `Set.prototype.forEach` has no early
exit, so this is unconditionally O(current Set size) on every call, giving O(n²) total work
for n such headers.

## Proof of Concept

The sharpest reproduction needs no unrelated keys at all — just N array-of-tables headers with
N *distinct* names, since nothing is ever pruned when no name repeats:

```js
const toml = require('toml');

function distinctArrayHeaders(n) {
  let out = '';
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) out += `[[a${i}]]\nv = 1\n`;
  return out;
}

// ~321 KB input -- takes ~10.3 seconds
toml.parse(distinctArrayHeaders(20000));
```

Measured timings (Node, direct execution against this repo):

| Variant | n | input size | time |
|---|---|---|---|
| N distinct-named `[[name]]` headers, no unrelated keys | 20,000 | 321 KB | 10.3 s |
| Same N with all-same-name headers (self-pruning, control) | 20,000 | 240 KB | 78 ms |
| M unrelated top-level keys + N same-name `[[name]]` headers | M=N=32,000 | 906 KB | 42.3 s |

The ~130x gap between the distinct-name and same-name cases at identical N and comparable
input size isolates the mechanism precisely: the bug is unbounded Set growth from never-pruned
entries, not string length or any other confound. A product-law check (varying M and N
independently in the mixed variant) further confirmed genuine O(M·N) complexity.

## Impact

Node.js is single-threaded — this synchronous, multi-second-to-tens-of-seconds compile blocks
the entire process event loop, standard uncontested Node.js behavior. The triggering document
shape — flat top-level config keys plus one or more array-of-tables sections (e.g. a `[db]`
settings block plus a `[[servers]]` list) — is unremarkable, common real-world TOML, not an
edge case. No authentication or special access is required; only the ability to get one TOML
string parsed by an application using this library.

## Suggested remediation

Avoid scanning the entire `assignedPaths`/`valueAssignments` Sets on every `[[name]]` header.
Index entries by their top-level path segment (e.g. a `Map<string, Set<string>>` keyed by the
first key component) so `addTableArray()` only ever scans the bucket relevant to the path
being reopened, in time proportional to that bucket's size rather than the whole document's
accumulated path count:

```js
var assignedByRoot = new Map(); // root segment -> Set<fullPath>

function addTableArray(node) {
  var path = node.value;
  var root = path[0];
  var bucket = assignedByRoot.get(root) || new Set();
  bucket.forEach(function(p) {
    if (isSameOrSubPath(p, quotedPath)) bucket.delete(p);
  });
  // ...rest of addTableArray unchanged, reading/writing the per-root bucket
  // instead of the global assignedPaths/valueAssignments Sets
}
```

As with the sibling finding, an input-size or table-count limit would also help as
defense-in-depth.

## Credit

Discovered and reported by SecDim Security Research
secdim.com | @secdim | security@secdim.com

title: nbconvert: Arbitrary file write through path traversal in cell output filenames when exporting to md, latex, rst and asciidoc
desc:
### Summary

nbconvert <= v7.17.1 has an arbitrary file write vulnerability due to a path traversal in ipynb cell output metadata, more specifically on the filename attribute.

Vulnerable converters : `--to markdown`, `--to latex`, `--to rst`, `--to asciidoc`.

In `ExtractOutputPreprocessor`, `extractoutput.py:116-119` joins attacker-controlled  `path` to `output_files_dir` with no canonicalization check, enabling arbitrary file write.

This is a sibling vulnerability of https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4c99-qj7h-p3vg.

### Impact

If a victim runs nbconvert on a malicious ipynb file, it can create some files with arbitrary data in arbitrary locations, i.e. override authorized_keys.

Note that running the cell with jupyter overrides the output, so it would "clean up" malicious cells.

### PoC

In a ipynb file:

```json

"cells": [{
        "cell_type": "code", "id": "abc123", "execution_count": 1,
        "metadata": {}, "source": "# PoC",
        "outputs": [{
            "output_type": "display_data",
            "metadata": {
                "filename": "../../../tmp/PWNED.png"  # ← traverses outside output_dir
            },
            "data": {
                # minimal valid PNG (1×1 pixel)
                "image/png": "iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAYAAAAfFcSJAAAADUlEQVR42mNk+M9QDwADhgGAWjR9awAAAABJRU5ErkJggg=="
            }
        }]
    }]

```


### Patches

Fixed in 
- https://github.com/jupyter/nbconvert/commit/ce4bd99aec31d81d759fa8eeb8643179392ec66f
- [7.17.2](https://github.com/jupyter/nbconvert/releases/tag/v7.17.2)

title: Sentry-Javascript: Middleware Bypass when using Tunnel route
desc:
### Impact

The `tunnelRoute` option makes the SDK send browser events to a path on your own Next.js server (for example `/monitoring`), where a rewrite forwards them to Sentry to prevent ad blockers from blocking them. To keep those envelope requests from being rejected by your middleware, the SDK skips middleware for them.

The middleware skip was wider than the rewrite. The rewrite only serves requests to the tunnel path itself with the `o` and `p` parameters set. The skip applied to anything under the tunnel path. Requests in that gap go to your application instead of Sentry, and your middleware never runs on them.

Skipping middleware does not grant the request any privileges. Routes that check the session server-side are still protected.

You are affected only if **all** of the following are true:

1. `tunnelRoute` is set (a string path or `true`),
2. your app is built with **webpack** (Turbopack builds are not affected),
3. some route of your application resolves under the tunnel path. That could be a direct collision (`/monitoring/foo` with `tunnelRoute: '/monitoring'`) or a dynamic segment at the route root (`app/[locale]/…`), which matches any first path segment, and
4. your middleware is the only place that enforces authorization for those routes.

Sentry's own services, and the data in your Sentry organization, are not affected.

### Patches

Fixed in [9.47.2](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/releases/tag/9.47.2), [10.75.2](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/releases/tag/10.75.2) and [11.0.0-rc.1](https://github.com/getsentry/sentry-javascript/releases/tag/11.0.0-rc.1). The skip now matches only the requests the tunnel rewrite actually serves. No configuration change is needed.

### Workarounds

- Set `tunnelRoute` to a path no route of yours can resolve under, or remove the option.
- Build with Turbopack (default for `next build` from Next.js 16).
- Enforce authorization in the route, layout or data-access path as well as in middleware.

title: Django REST framework: Accept header with many large quoted parameters burns ~19s of CPU per request in content negotiation
desc:
### Summary

DRF's content negotiation parses each Accept token several times per request and never limits the number of tokens or their total size. Each parse ends up in Django's parse_header_parameters, which takes quadratic time when a quoted parameter value is packed with semicolons. On my machine a single GET with a 780KB Accept header made of 96 such tokens kept one gunicorn worker busy for 18.87 seconds (Django 6.1, djangorestframework 3.18.0, gunicorn 26.0.0, Python 3.13, Docker on macOS). The header is syntactically valid, fits inside gunicorn's default header limits, and needs no authentication. Two concurrent requests, which is one per sync worker, made a default two worker deployment stop answering for my whole 40 second test window. It recovered half a second after I stopped sending.


### Details

#### What happens

get_accept_list() splits the Accept header on commas with no cap on token count or total size, at rest_framework/negotiation.py:96-97.

For every token, select_renderer() calls media_type_matches() once per renderer, and each call builds fresh _MediaType objects for both sides, at rest_framework/negotiation.py:53-56 and rest_framework/utils/mediatypes.py:22-23. `_MediaType.__init__` calls django.utils.http.parse_header_parameters unconditionally, at rest_framework/utils/mediatypes.py:47.

When nothing matches, DRF raises NotAcceptable (406). Rendering that error response also needs a renderer, so finalize_response() runs the entire negotiation a second time through perform_content_negotiation(force=True), at rest_framework/views.py:434-437.

With the default two renderers this comes to about six parses per Accept token per request. I confirmed the count by instrumenting _MediaType with a counter: six per token, three from the normal pass and three from the forced re-negotiation.

The quadratic part is on the Django side. parse_header_parameters splits parameters with _parseparam, which handles quoted values by recounting the quote characters from the start of the string for every candidate separator, the s.count('"', 0, end) calls in django/utils/http.py. A quoted value holding k semicolons costs roughly k rescans over k characters, so a single ~8KB value takes about 31ms per parse here.

Numbers from my runs, measured as utime+stime deltas of the server process:

one token, ~9KB: 230ms server CPU
24 tokens, 216KB: 5.07s on runserver, which has no per field limit
48 tokens, 432KB: 10.08s on runserver
96 tokens, 780KB: 18.87s under gunicorn defaults

Wall time matched CPU time in every run, so this is pure CPU work. RSS stayed flat at 57MB throughout, this is a time attack and not a memory one.

#### A few details that matter for reproducing it:

Django rejects a single media type string longer than 10,000 chars (MAX_HEADER_LENGTH), so each token has to stay just under that. Going over gives you a ValueError and a 500, which is a different and much weaker problem.

gunicorn defaults are limit_request_field_size 8190 and limit_request_fields 100, so the working shape is 96 separate Accept fields with one ~8.1KB token each. That puts the single request ceiling near 19s, below the default 30s worker timeout, so one request alone does not get a stock gunicorn worker killed by the arbiter. It does not need to. Each request pins one sync worker for its full duration, so on two workers, two held connections wedge the service.

order_by_precedence collects tokens into a set, so identical tokens collapse and the cost mostly disappears. Each token needs its own parameter name, x0=, x1=, x2= and so on.

#### Where a fix could go, either of these alone would be enough:

Parse each Accept token once per request and reuse the result in the matching loop and in the 406 re-negotiation.

Put an aggregate budget in get_accept_list(), say 8KB total or 64 tokens, and treat anything past it as not acceptable.

The quadratic behavior itself lives in Django's parser, but DRF is the one calling it six times per token with no cap on how many tokens there are, so both fixes look like DRF changes to me.


### PoC

Verified end to end on Docker Desktop for macOS (Apple Silicon, 8 cores), python:3.13-slim image, Django 6.1, djangorestframework 3.18.0, gunicorn 26.0.0. Nothing was configured beyond defaults.

Minimal target, any default DRF project works, this is the one I used.

requirements.txt:

    django==6.1
    djangorestframework==3.18.0
    gunicorn==26.0.0

pocproj/settings.py:
```python
SECRET_KEY = 'poc'; DEBUG = False; ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['*']
INSTALLED_APPS = ['django.contrib.contenttypes', 'django.contrib.auth', 'rest_framework']
ROOT_URLCONF = 'pocproj.urls'; WSGI_APPLICATION = 'pocproj.wsgi.application'
DATABASES = {'default': {'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.sqlite3', 'NAME': ':memory:'}}
USE_TZ = True
```

pocproj/api.py:
```python
from rest_framework.views import APIView
from rest_framework.response import Response

class Items(APIView):
    def get(self, request):
        return Response([{'id': 1, 'name': 'ok'}])
```

pocproj/urls.py:
